Lessons.Title: Solving Trigonometric Equations with Identities
ExplanationParagraphs: Identities hold for all inputs in the common domain of the two expressions. Equations may instead hold only for particular inputs.
Fundamental Pythagorean: sin²t+cos²t=1; 1+tan²t=sec²t where cos t≠0; 1+cot²t=csc²t where sin t≠0.
Reciprocal: sec=1/cos, csc=1/sin; quotient tan=sin/cos, cot=cos/sin. Preserve original denominator exclusions when simplifying.
Cos and sec are even; sin, tan, cot, csc are odd, on their domains. Use these identities to transform negative angles.
Algebraic proof uses factoring, expanding, common denominators, and conjugates; checking individual numeric inputs only disproves false identities.
Independent Cool-down: simplify (1−cos²t)/sin²t, simplify sec²t−tan²t and disprove sin t+cos t=1 universally.
Independent Try It 2: Simplify csc t sin t
Independent Try It 5: Express sec²t with tan²t

KeyConcepts.Title: Function parity
KeyConcepts.Rule: Replace negative input with correct sign.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proof vs example
KeyConcepts.Rule: Numerical counterexample disproves but numerical agreement doesn't prove.
KeyConcepts.Example: sin t+cos t=1 fails at π/4

Visuals.Description: Mathematically authored table of identities and domains.

SummaryPoints: Preserve domain in every trig cancellation.
Algebra proves identities; a counterexample disproves.
Use reciprocal, Pythagorean and parity laws.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accepting an answer without validating the original problem conditions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An algebraic candidate can violate a given domain, interval, sign, model assumption or unit restriction.
